meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In His will is our peace'?
meta.ogDescription: A rare true one: Dante wrote it. Paradiso, Canto III, line 85, spoken by Piccarda Donati — "E 'n la sua volontade è nostra pace."

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1265–1321 · Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine line of Dante’s. It is verse 85 of Paradiso, Canto III — “E ’n la sua volontade è nostra pace” — spoken by the soul of Piccarda Donati in the Heaven of the Moon. “In His will is our peace” is the standard, faithful English rendering of that half-line.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Divine Comedy — Paradiso, Canto III, line 85
Piccarda Donati, in the Heaven of the Moon

source.excerpt:
E ’n la sua volontade è nostra pace:
ella è quel mare al qual tutto si move
ciò ch’ella crïa o che natura face.

“And in His will is our peace: it is that sea to which all things move, both what it creates and what nature makes.”
trail: The line is Piccarda’s in Paradiso III.85; Wikipedia records the Italian and its standard English as “In la sua volontade è nostra pace (In his will is our peace); Paradiso, III.85.”
Wikiquote’s sourced Dante page lists the verse under The Divine Comedy, rendering it “And his will is our peace.”
A. S. Kline’s complete translation gives the line in context as “in his will is our peace … it is the sea, to which all things flow.”
source.excerptNote: Piccarda answers Dante’s question of whether the souls in the lowest sphere of Heaven wish they were higher: they do not, because their will is wholly aligned with God’s. Matthew Arnold singled out the Italian line as a “touchstone” of the highest poetry.

source.rightsNote: Dante wrote the Paradiso around 1316–1321, so the original Italian is long in the public domain. “In His will is our peace” is the standard, near-verbatim literal English of a six-word half-line, and appears freely in public-domain sources (e.g. Matthew Arnold’s 1880 “The Study of Poetry”); it is not the distinctive expression of any single modern translator. A full modern verse translation of the whole poem, however, may itself be under copyright.

author.name: Dante Alighieri
author.heading: About the author
author.metaLine: 1265–1321 · Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy
author.bio: Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet whose three-part Divine Comedy (Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso) is the founding masterwork of Italian literature. In Paradiso III he meets Piccarda Donati, a nun forced from her convent, who explains that the blessed feel no envy of higher souls because their wills rest wholly in God’s — the thought crystallised in this line. The verse echoes Augustine’s “our heart is restless until it rests in Thee.”

misattribution.heading: A note on wording
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is right — this is one of the genuine Dante lines. The only thing worth flagging is that the familiar English is a translation, so its exact wording shifts from edition to edition.

items.why: The Italian is fixed — “E ’n la sua volontade è nostra pace” — but translators render it variously: “And his will is our peace” (Longfellow), “in his will is our peace” (Kline), and the compressed pull-quote form “In His will, our peace” that circulates on quote sites. All are faithful to the same line.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: genuinely Dante — Paradiso III.85, spoken by Piccarda Donati. Only the English phrasing varies by translator; the line and its author are secure. See Wikipedia.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Piccarda’s answer resolves the central puzzle of Dante’s Heaven: if some souls stand nearer God than others, do the lower ones feel slighted? No, she says — in blessedness the will is so conformed to God’s that there is nothing left to want. Peace is not resignation but the disappearance of any gap between one’s own desire and the divine will.

The line became a touchstone of European letters. Matthew Arnold quoted it as an example of poetry of the very highest order, and T. S. Eliot returned to it in his essay on Dante — which is much of why a half-line from a fourteenth-century canto still circulates as a standalone maxim today.
